about: The codex's 'by rule' tier (Bench plan B2, docs/loop/items/I-056/spec.md). Generated by tools/chemdb/build_rules.py; edit that script, not this file. Every reaction comes from one of the rules below, applied to the tables below (ions, salts, solubility, reactivity series, acids, fuels), and never shadows a checked core reaction (no rule reaction has the reactants of a core one). tier 'rule' and check 'draft' until the science review of a sample. dh_kj is the reaction's standard enthalpy change from the substances' enthalpies of formation, which sets heat. bottles lists the bottles the tier adds to the Bench shelf and the band each first appears at.

sources.OPENSTAX-SOL: OpenStax Chemistry 2e (2019), section 4.2, Table 4.1 'Solubilities of Common Ionic Compounds in Water' (https://openstax.org/books/chemistry-2e/pages/4-2-classifying-chemical-reactions); slightly soluble salts (CaSO4, Ag2SO4, PbCl2, Ca(OH)2, Li2CO3, MgCO3) are marked slight and never used as a precipitate or a dissolved reactant.
sources.CRC-ECS: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 'Electrochemical Series' (P. Vanysek), standard reduction potentials E (V) at 298.15 K: Li+ -3.04, K+ -2.93, Ba2+ -2.91, Ca2+ -2.87, Na+ -2.71, Mg2+ -2.37, Al3+ -1.66, Zn2+ -0.76, Fe2+ -0.45, Pb2+ -0.13, H+ 0, Cu2+ +0.34, Ag+ +0.80.
sources.OPENSTAX-ACID: OpenStax Chemistry 2e (2019), section 4.2 'Acid-Base Reactions' and section 14 'Acid-Base Equilibria': an acid and a base give a salt and water; metal oxides and hydroxides are bases; ammonia is a base that gives the ammonium salt.
sources.OPENSTAX-COMB: OpenStax Chemistry 2e (2019), section 4.2 'Combustion reactions': a hydrocarbon or other C, H, O fuel burning in plenty of oxygen gives carbon dioxide and water.
sources.OPENSTAX-REDOX: OpenStax Chemistry 2e (2019), section 4.2 'Single-displacement (replacement) reactions' and section 17.3 'Standard reduction potentials'.
sources.GHS: Hazard classes as in each substance's GHS classification (PubChem Laboratory Chemical Safety Summary), judged at the concentration a Bench bottle holds (dilute acids up to 1 M and alkalis up to 0.4 M are low hazard: CLEAPSS Hazcards); lead compounds (reproductive toxicity 1A), soluble barium compounds (acute toxicity), mercury, silver nitrate (corrosive, stains skin) and quicklime (corrosive solid, reacts hot with water) stay lab.
sources.CRC-PKA: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 'Dissociation Constants of Inorganic Acids' and 'of Organic Acids and Bases', pKa at 25 C: HSO4- 1.99; H3PO4 2.15, H2PO4- 7.20, HPO4-2 12.35; H2CO3 6.35, HCO3- 10.33; CH3COOH 4.76; NH4+ 9.25. A base takes a proton only from an acid at least as strong as its own conjugate acid, so carbonate cannot make phosphate (PO4-3) and ammonia stops at hydrogenphosphate.
sources.PASSIVE: Greenwood and Earnshaw, Chemistry of the Elements (2nd ed.), section 7.3: aluminium's Al2O3 film stops it reacting with sulfate or nitrate solutions and with cold dilute sulfuric acid; chloride (or bromide) breaks the film (RSC Education, 'Aluminium and copper sulfate: the role of chloride').
sources.BASIC-CARB: Greenwood and Earnshaw, Chemistry of the Elements (2nd ed.), sections 28.3.4 and 29.3.2: copper(II) and zinc ions with a carbonate solution give basic carbonates (Cu2(OH)2CO3, Zn5(CO3)2(OH)6) and carbon dioxide, not CuCO3 or ZnCO3; with ammonium carbonate (which carries free ammonia) silver, copper and zinc form soluble ammine complexes, and ammoniacal silver can deposit explosive silver nitride.
sources.FLASH: PubChem / NIOSH Pocket Guide flash points (closed cup): heptane -4 C, cyclohexane -20 C, nonane 31 C, decane 46 C, undecane 60 C, dodecane 71 C, hexadecane 135 C, 1-butanol 35 C, 1-pentanol 49 C; propene, butene, pentene (-18 C) and propyne are gases or very volatile. A spark lights a liquid only above its flash point; below it the fuel must be heated (or burn on a wick).

rules.name: acid + base
rules.text: An acid and a base neutralise (cancel out) each other, making a salt and water (ammonia makes the salt alone).

rules.name: metal + acid
rules.text: A metal above hydrogen in the reactivity series pushes hydrogen out of an acid, making a salt and hydrogen gas (not nitric acid, which makes brown poisonous gases instead).

rules.name: carbonate + acid
rules.text: A carbonate or hydrogencarbonate fizzes in an acid, making a salt, water and carbon dioxide.

rules.name: fuel burns
rules.text: A fuel made of carbon and hydrogen (and sometimes oxygen) burns in plenty of oxygen to make carbon dioxide and water.

rules.name: two salts swap
rules.text: Two dissolved salts swap partners; the new pair that cannot dissolve in water (the solubility rules) comes out as a solid.

rules.name: metal swap
rules.text: A more reactive metal pushes a less reactive metal out of a solution of its salt (the reactivity series).

excluded: F-, HF, CN-, ClO4-, CrO4-2, Cr2O7-2, Hg2+ and Hg+2 salts, explosive products

species.AgNO3: silver nitrate burns and stains skin
species.CaO: quicklime is corrosive and gets hot with water

reactions.name: Quicklime and vinegar
reactions.say: Vinegar neutralises quicklime, giving calcium acetate and water.
